chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Zurara from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding the matter that the petitioner seeks from his Lord.

He said: 'Give charity during your day to sixty poor people; for each poor person, one sa' (measure), by the sa' of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). When it becomes night, you perform ghusl (ritual bath) in the remaining third of the night, and wear the cheapest clothing that one wears for their dependents, except that you must wear an izar (lower garment) with that clothing. Then you pray two rak'ahs.'
When you place your forehead in the final prostration for prostration, you glorify God, magnify Him, honor Him, and sanctify Him, and you mention your sins, thereby confessing to them by name.
Then you raise your head. Then when you place your head for the second prostration, you ask God for guidance (istikhara) one hundred times - 'O God, I ask You for guidance.'

Then you supplicate to God with whatever you wish, then you ask Him. And whenever you prostrate, press your knees to the ground, then lift the izar until you expose them, and place the izar behind you between your buttocks and the inner part of your shins.'

key_terms.إِزَاراً: A lower garment or loincloth worn during prayer.
key_terms.اِسْتَخَرْتَ: You ask for divine guidance or choice (istikhara).
key_terms.بَاطِنِ سَاقَيْكَ: The inner part of your shins.
key_terms.صَاعٌ: A specific volume measure used for charity, equivalent to the Prophet's measure.

ai.seo_question: What is the ritual procedure for Salat al-Mudtir to fulfill a specific need?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* from the chain of Zurarah, this hadith details the ritual of Salat al-Mudtir, emphasizing the connection between material purification through charity (sadaqah) and spiritual humility. The specific instruction to expose the knees during prostration serves as a physical manifestation of modesty and readiness before God, reflecting the Shia emphasis on precise bodily etiquette (adab) in supplication.
